paras: The lynching of William Moore took place early on June 26, 1888, when a mob of armed men broke into the jail at Charleston, Coles County, Illinois, and hanged Moore, a Black man from Mattoon, from the water tank near the depot. He had been accused of assaulting a young white woman, Mary A. Bumgardner, and was being held for the grand jury. Within days, dispatches from her home district called her of bad repute and Moore innocent, and in October nine men were indicted.

Moore was described as a married man of about 43 with four children. According to the first dispatches, on the preceding Saturday night a young woman arriving by train asked him for directions at the depot, and he led her instead to an isolated spot and assaulted her. Papers gave her age as 16, 17 or "about nineteen or twenty" and her home as Effingham, Shelbyville or near Altamont. On Monday Squire McFadden held Moore in $1,000 bail, and because of "talk of summary vengeance" he was moved that night to the county jail at Charleston.

Late that night, the Rock Island Argus reported, a party of men boarded a freight train at Mattoon over the conductor's objections and rode to Charleston. About 1 a.m. the men, given as 200 in one account and 150 in another, seized the jail and the sheriff and broke through the iron doors with sledge hammers, while the sheriff and the state's attorney urged them in vain to stop.

At the water tank Moore denied his guilt, sang a hymn in which the crowd joined, and prayed. According to the Argus, he "acknowledged" taking the girl from the depot "for immoral purposes" while still denying the assault, and was then hanged. The sheriff cut the body down after twenty-five minutes, and some of the lynchers warned that several Black residents of Charleston and Mattoon should leave.

On June 27 an Altamont dispatch to the Indianapolis Journal said the accuser was "of very bad repute" and had left to escape prosecution for burning a barn, and that local people were confident Moore was innocent. A Mattoon report of July 2 called her story "contradictory" and noted talk of prosecuting the lynchers.

On July 13 Judge Hughes ordered a special court term, and a grand jury impaneled on August 4 returned nine indictments in early October. The Indianapolis Journal named the men as J. B. Benesiel, H. M. O. Thode, L. D. Weaver, John Byers, William Kincaid, B. Brewer, S. H. Kirkpatrick, Adolf Walker and Eli Myers, one of them a former mayor. Three gave heavy bonds for the November term while others had left, and on December 6 Kirkpatrick was reported acquitted; no outcome for the others was found.

The first short wire, stating the assault as fact, ran June 26 and 27 in Texas, Georgia and Washington; the San Antonio Daily Light headed it "Meets His Deserts." The same text ran as late as July 21 in Wyoming as "They Settled the Coon," and an Elko, Nevada, column called the hanging "Swift, correct and cheap justice." The fuller Charleston dispatch, headed "A Negro Rapist Hanged by a Mob" in Maysville, Kentucky, still reported that "All here condemn the act."

The Rock Island Argus headlined "Mob Law in Illinois" while relaying the lynchers' wish to avoid "the law's delay." After the Altamont reports, "Innocent Man Lynched" ran in Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio, and the Telegram-Herald wrote that "Illegal short cuts are bad roads." In October the Brookings County Sentinel wrote that "the mob had been guilty of murder," and the Lexington Dispatch in South Carolina said the citizens should have "allowed the law to take its course."

Most reports placed the mob's origin in Mattoon, but one wire named Mattoon, Shelbyville and Effingham, and a Mattoon report implicated the "best citizens" of Charleston. The Charleston wire said "scarcely any concealment of identity was attempted," while the Argus said the lynchers were masked and unrecognized. The Abilene version said Moore had been "convicted," against accounts that he was only held for the grand jury, and the indictment dispatch dated the lynching June 25 rather than June 26.

accounts.label: First wire (Charleston via Chicago/St. Louis)
accounts.gist: Moore, who 'assaulted' a sixteen-year-old girl at Mattoon, was taken from the Charleston jail and lynched by masked men.

accounts.label: Fuller Charleston dispatch
accounts.gist: Two hundred armed men took the jail and sheriff, broke in with sledge hammers, gave Moore ten minutes and hanged him at the depot tank; the town condemned it but no prosecution was expected.

accounts.label: Rock Island Argus correspondent
accounts.gist: Detailed narrative of the freight-train ride from Mattoon, masked lynchers, Moore's denial and partial admission, the hymn, the hanging, and threats against other Black residents.

accounts.label: Mattoon dispatch, June 27
accounts.gist: Moore of Mattoon was held in $1,000 bond and taken to Charleston by the city marshal; the girl's friends from Shelbyville and Effingham rode the 11 p.m. train; masked men broke three iron doors.

accounts.label: Altamont dispatches
accounts.gist: The accuser was of bad repute, older than reported and fleeing an arson prosecution; locals believed Moore innocent.

accounts.label: Indictment dispatch, October
accounts.gist: Nine Mattoon citizens indicted; a deputy had been warned by telegram; 150 armed, masked men broke into the jail.

framing.detail: First-wire headlines 'Meets His Deserts', 'They Settled the Coon', and Elko's 'Swift, correct and cheap justice' stated the assault as fact and approved.
Most early papers ran the short wire as a brief, sometimes paired with the Ned Clark lynching in Georgia.
The fuller dispatch called Moore a 'wretch' and the girl 'of good reputation' but reported 'All here condemn the act.'
Rock Island Argus headed 'Mob Law in Illinois ... one more lawless deed' while presenting the lynchers' reasoning about 'the law's delay'.
After the Altamont reports: 'Hanged for a Crime He Did Not Commit', 'Innocent Man Lynched', 'The Beauty of Mob Law', and editorials on the evils of lynch law.
October editorial notes: 'the mob had been guilty of murder'; better to 'rely upon the law'.
Marietta Journal used an apparently related item to say Westerners, like Southerners, would not tolerate 'the usual offense'.

conflicts.note: Most contemporary reports give early Tuesday, June 26; 'June 25' and 'Monday' likely refer to the night before.
The Hocking Sentinel's 'Watton' is the same wire as Maysville's 'Mattoon', an OCR or typesetting variant; indicted men were of Mattoon.
The Altamont dispatches come from her home district.
The Argus is ambiguous; Moore was arrested at his home in Mattoon.
